unit.title: Energy, aero and performance in 2026
unit.summary: Where the battery gives lap time, when the wings open, and how teams develop the car.

lessons.title: Energy across a lap
lessons.objective: Explain where a car deploys and where it harvests.

payload.prompt: Where on a lap does a driver deploy electrical power?

options.text: Mainly on straights and exits to gain top speed or help traction.
options.explanation: Right. Deployment helps most on straights (speed) and corner exits (traction). Braking and turning don't need it.

options.text: Under braking to help slow the car down faster.
options.explanation: No. Braking harvests energy; deployment makes the car faster, not slower.

options.text: Through the entire lap equally.
options.explanation: No, energy is finite. Teams pick the spots where deployment gains the most time.

options.text: Only when overtaking another car.
options.explanation: Overtake Mode is for when within one second, but deployment also helps on solo laps.

explanation.correct: Right. Drivers deploy energy where it gains the most time: straights for speed, exits for traction.
explanation.incorrect: Deployment is used on straights (speed) and exits (traction). Braking is for harvesting, not deploying.
explanation.sayThisLine: The battery helps on straights and exits.

payload.prompt: What limits how much electrical power a 2026 driver can use in one lap?

options.text: The battery size and the per-lap deployment limits set by the FIA.
options.explanation: Right. Each team has a fixed energy budget per lap they cannot exceed, even if the battery is full.

options.text: How much they harvested in that same lap.
options.explanation: Related, but the limit is FIA-set. You can deploy more than you harvest if the battery has reserve.

options.text: The driver's physical fitness.
options.explanation: That affects braking force, not electrical deployment.

options.text: Nothing; drivers can deploy unlimited power.
options.explanation: No, there are strict per-lap limits to keep racing fair.

explanation.correct: Right. The FIA sets a per-lap deployment limit. Every team gets the same budget; strategy is how they spend it.
explanation.incorrect: The FIA sets strict per-lap electrical deployment limits so teams cannot just dump the whole battery in one lap.

lessons.title: Clipping and super-clipping
lessons.objective: Explain why a car slows at the end of a straight and what teams do about it.

payload.prompt: What happens when a 2026 car clips (runs out of battery)?

options.text: The car stops getting electrical power, slows visibly, and is forced to harvest instead of deploy.
options.explanation: Right. Clipping is the car running out of energy. It then prioritises harvesting to refill.

options.text: The engine automatically shuts off.
options.explanation: No, the combustion engine stays on. Only the electrical assist stops.

options.text: The car crashes if it clips.
options.explanation: No, clipping just means the battery is empty. The car is slower but safe.

options.text: A penalty is given for over-deploying.
options.explanation: Clipping is not a penalty. It is a strategy consequence: you ran out early.

explanation.correct: Right. Clipping is when the battery empties. The car loses electrical help and even loses speed as it forces a harvest.
explanation.incorrect: Clipping happens when the battery runs out. The car stops accelerating and must harvest energy to refill.

payload.prompt: Why is clipping on a long straight bad for a driver's lap time?

options.text: The car stops accelerating and even slows while harvesting, costing crucial top speed on the straight.
options.explanation: Right. A straight is where you need top speed; clipping there is costly. Better to clip on a braking zone.

options.text: It requires the driver to brake early.
options.explanation: Clipping doesn't force braking. The car just stops gaining speed.

options.text: It damages the battery.
options.explanation: Clipping does not damage the battery. It just empties it.

options.text: The tyre loses grip.
options.explanation: Clipping doesn't affect tyres; it only affects electrical power and speed.

explanation.correct: Right. Clipping at the end of a straight kills top speed. Teams aim to clip under braking instead.
explanation.incorrect: Clipping on a straight is bad because the car loses the electrical boost just when it needs maximum speed.

lessons.title: When to open the wings
lessons.objective: Decide when to hold Straight Mode and when to close it.

payload.prompt: Should a driver close the wings (Corner Mode) before entering a high-speed corner?

scene.alt: A 2026 F1 car approaching a fast corner.

explanation.correct: Right. Close (high downforce) for the corner to grip; open (low drag) only on straights.
explanation.incorrect: Yes. Open wings reduce downforce and grip. Close them before the corner to help the car turn.

payload.prompt: Can a driver open Straight Mode (wings flat) only in FIA-approved zones?

scene.alt: A 2026 F1 car on a circuit showing wing zones.

explanation.correct: Right. Straight Mode is zone-restricted per circuit for safety and fairness.
explanation.incorrect: Yes. Straight Mode is only legal in FIA-designated zones, not the whole lap.

lessons.title: One lap on the battery
lessons.objective: Explain qualifying energy limits and how they shape a lap.

payload.prompt: In qualifying, do you lift-and-coast to recharge mid-lap, or push flat-out for one perfect lap?

situation.narrative: Qualifying Q3, your final lap. You are 0.15 seconds off the provisional pole. Your battery is at 50% and you have one chance.

options.label: Push flat-out and likely clip at the end
options.consequence: One perfect lap with maximum deployment now, even if you clip. A 0.15-second gain outweighs clipping.
considerations: Maximum power on every straight
You will clip mid-final-corner, costing no time (braking)
One shot to beat pole

options.label: Lift-and-coast to recharge and stay on battery
options.consequence: Stay flush the whole lap but lose deployment time, so no pole. Safer but slower.
considerations: No clipping risk
0.1-second loss from missing deployment at the end
Not enough to beat pole anyway

payload.expertNote: Qualifying is one lap. Energy management is secondary to outright pace. Push for pole and accept clipping if it means beating the rival.
payload.sayThisLine: In qualifying, one lap trumps energy planning.

payload.prompt: How does the 2026 battery role differ between qualifying and race?

situation.narrative: You need to understand why energy matters differently in a 70-lap race than a one-lap qualifying run.

facts.label: Qualifying energy rule
facts.value: Deploy it all for one perfect lap

facts.label: The difference
facts.value: Managing finite battery for 1 vs 70 laps

options.label: Qualifying is one-lap pace; races are pit-window and tyre strategy
options.consequence: Correct. Qualifying: push the battery hard and clip is fine. Races: manage it lap-by-lap and plan pit windows.
considerations: Energy management in races is like fuel strategy in years past
Qualifying: one lap, one battery budget
Races: preserve the battery across stints

options.label: The battery role is the same; just use less per lap
options.consequence: Close, but energy is managed differently. Qualifying is one-lap peak power; races are sustained pace.
considerations: True that you use less per lap in races
But the strategy is fundamentally different

payload.expertNote: Qualifying battery strategy is maximize-now. Race strategy is maximize-over-distance. The per-lap limit is the same, but the stakes change.
payload.sayThisLine: Qualifying: spend it all. Races: save it for when it matters.

lessons.title: Power unit politics
lessons.objective: Explain homologation-style upgrades and the ADUO safety net.

payload.prompt: What is ADUO in 2026 Formula 1?

options.text: Extra engine-upgrade chances for manufacturers that fall behind, assessed after certain races.
options.explanation: Right. ADUO (Additional Development Opportunities) is a safety net: if you are struggling, you get more upgrade slots.

options.text: A penalty for teams that exceed the cost cap.
options.explanation: No, ADUO is an aid to struggling manufacturers, not a penalty.

options.text: A ban on engine upgrades mid-season.
options.explanation: No, ADUO is the opposite: it allows extra upgrades for underperforming makers.

options.text: A power-unit noise regulation.
options.explanation: ADUO is about development, not sound regulation.

explanation.correct: Right. ADUO gives struggling engine makers extra upgrade opportunities after rounds 6, 12 and 18.
explanation.incorrect: ADUO is a safety valve: if a new engine maker falls behind, they get extra development time. It levels the playing field.

payload.prompt: What is PU allocation in F1?

options.text: A limited number of each power-unit element (engines, turbos, batteries) per season; extra parts incur grid penalties.
options.explanation: Right. Teams have a quota. Taking a seventh engine, for example, means a grid penalty at the next race.

options.text: An equal budget for all teams to build engines.
options.explanation: No, allocation is about the number of components. Budget is the cost cap.

options.text: A system that allows one team more power than others.
options.explanation: No, PU allocation restricts how many you can use, not how powerful they are.

options.text: A renewable resource that resets each race.
options.explanation: Allocation is per season, not per race. Taking a fresh engine uses up your allocation.

explanation.correct: Right. PU allocation limits how many of each power-unit component teams can use per season. Going over means grid penalties.
explanation.incorrect: PU allocation is a per-season quota on power-unit elements. Teams choose when to burn their allocation and accept the grid penalty.

payload.prompt: What was the 2026 compression-ratio row about?

options.text: A dispute over how to measure engine compression when the engine is hot versus cold.
options.explanation: Right. Some makers complained measuring cold alone was unfair; the FIA clarified to measure both.

options.text: A rule that all engines must have the same compression.
options.explanation: No, compression ratio is not standardised. The row was about how to measure it fairly.

options.text: A ban on using high-compression engines.
options.explanation: No, the dispute was about fair measurement, not banning high compression.

options.text: A cost associated with upgrading the engine.
options.explanation: Compression ratio is technical; it does not have a cost-cap impact.

explanation.correct: Right. The 2026 compression-ratio debate was technical: how do you measure compression fairly when engines heat and change?
explanation.incorrect: The 2026 compression-ratio argument was about measurement standards: should you measure cold or hot? The FIA clarified both.

payload.prompt: Match each 2026 engine maker to its story.

pairs.definition: Returning incumbent supplier; continues McLaren, Williams, Alpine; also runs its own team.
New works team and power-unit maker; may qualify for ADUO if early pace lags.
New engine supplier to Aston Martin in a works-style partnership; also eligible for ADUO.

distractorDefinitions: Continues to be the only engine supplier on the grid.
Banned from upgrading engines until round 6.

explanation.summary: Mercedes is the established player; Audi and Honda are new. ADUO helps new makers catch up.
explanation.sayThisLine: 2026 has three engine makers fighting a reset.

lessons.title: Aero development and tunnel time
lessons.objective: Explain ATR, flexi-wings and technical directives.

payload.prompt: What is ATR (aero testing restrictions)?

options.text: A sliding scale of wind-tunnel and CFD time based on last season's standings: worse teams get more time to develop.
options.explanation: Right. It is a handicap system: if you finished last, you get more testing to catch up.

options.text: A ban on aerodynamic testing during the race.
options.explanation: No, ATR is about development time in the season, not race restrictions.

options.text: An equal amount of testing time for all teams.
options.explanation: Wrong: it is a sliding scale. Fast teams get less, slow teams get more.

options.text: A requirement to use only one wind tunnel.
options.explanation: ATR is about the time limit, not which facilities you use.

explanation.correct: Right. Aero testing restrictions are a handicap: finishing last last year means more wind-tunnel time this year.
explanation.incorrect: ATR is a sliding scale of development time to help slower teams catch up to faster ones.

payload.prompt: What is a flexi-wing in F1?

options.text: A wing that bends under load to reduce drag while passing static tests, a recurring loophole teams exploit.
options.explanation: Right. Teams design wings that flex during racing but look rigid in the garage. The FIA keeps closing the loophole.

options.text: A deliberately adjustable wing that drivers change during a race.
options.explanation: No, flexi-wings are accidental or hidden bending, not intentional adjustment like active aero.

options.text: A wing banned since 2020.
options.explanation: Flexi-wings were not banned; teams still try to exploit them. The FIA is always fighting the loophole.

options.text: A wing made of rubber that absorbs impacts.
options.explanation: No, flexi-wings are carbon-fibre wings that bend strategically under aerodynamic load.

explanation.correct: Right. Flexi-wings bend during high-speed running, cutting drag, yet pass static tests in the garage.
explanation.incorrect: A flexi-wing is a structural loophole: the wing bends in the air to reduce drag but looks fixed when tested stationary.

payload.prompt: What is a technical directive (TD) in F1?

options.text: An FIA clarification on how rules will be policed, used to close loopholes mid-season.
options.explanation: Right. TDs are not rule changes; they are clarifications of intent, often closing tricks like flexi-wings.

options.text: A penalty handed to teams for rule breaches.
options.explanation: No, TDs are preventative clarifications, not penalties.

options.text: A new rule that replaces the old rulebook.
options.explanation: No, TDs are minor clarifications within the existing rules, not rule changes.

options.text: A directive telling teams which engine to use.
options.explanation: TDs are about technical interpretation, not engine choice.

explanation.correct: Right. A technical directive clarifies how the FIA will police a rule, often to close a loophole quickly.
explanation.incorrect: Technical directives are FIA clarifications on rules, not rule changes. They close loopholes and prevent teams from gaming the regs.

payload.prompt: Match each aerodynamic issue to how it is handled.

pairs.definition: A recurring loophole where wings bend under load to cut drag. The FIA updates the rules and issues technical directives to prevent it.
An FIA clarification issued quickly mid-season to close a loophole like flexi-wings without rewriting the whole rulebook.

distractorDefinitions: A new wing that is faster than others.
A penalty for teams caught cheating.

explanation.summary: Flexi-wings are the loophole; technical directives are how the FIA fights back quickly.
explanation.sayThisLine: TDs close loopholes like flexi-wings mid-season.

lessons.title: The cost cap and how teams spend
lessons.objective: Explain the cap and why it matters to competitiveness.

payload.prompt: What is the F1 cost cap?

options.text: A yearly limit (roughly $215 million) on team spending, with big carve-outs for driver salaries and marketing.
options.explanation: Right. Teams can spend a fixed amount per year; exceeding it brings fines and sporting penalties.

options.text: An equal budget for all teams.
options.explanation: No, the cap is a limit, not an equal grant. Teams fundraise independently.

options.text: A ban on expensive components.
options.explanation: No, teams can buy any part. The cap limits total spending.

options.text: A regulation that started in the 1980s.
options.explanation: The modern cost cap started in 2021, not in the 1980s.

explanation.correct: Right. The cost cap is roughly $215 million per year per team. Breaches bring points deductions and fines.
explanation.incorrect: The cost cap is an annual spending ceiling. Exceeding it earns penalties, including points deductions.

payload.prompt: Why does the cost cap matter for racing fairness?

options.text: It prevents the richest teams from spending unlimited money and crushing the competition.
options.explanation: Right. Without a cap, Ferrari or Mercedes could outspend everyone. The cap keeps the grid more even.

options.text: It reduces the quality of cars and makes racing slower.
options.explanation: Capping spending doesn't slow cars; teams still innovate within the limit.

options.text: It forces teams to buy cheaper parts.
options.explanation: The cap limits total spending, not part cost. Teams prioritise what matters most.

options.text: It has no real impact on the grid.
options.explanation: The cap has a huge impact: it keeps small teams competitive against billionaire budgets.

explanation.correct: Right. The cost cap keeps spending in check so a smaller team can compete against a rich one.
explanation.incorrect: The cost cap prevents unlimited spending from turning F1 into a billionaire-only arms race.

payload.prompt: What happens if a team exceeds the cost cap?

options.text: Fines and sporting penalties including points deductions or a ban from some races.
options.explanation: Right. The FIA can fine, deduct points or ban the team for a breach.

options.text: They are forced to refund the excess money.
options.explanation: No, penalties are fines and sporting sanctions, not refunds.

options.text: Nothing; the cap is voluntary.
options.explanation: No, the cap is mandatory. Breaches have real consequences.

options.text: The driver is banned from the next race.
options.explanation: Penalties are team penalties, not driver bans.

explanation.correct: Right. Cost-cap breaches draw big fines and can trigger points deductions or race bans.
explanation.incorrect: Teams that exceed the cost cap face fines and sporting penalties such as points deductions.

payload.prompt: Guess the F1 cost cap per team per year, in US dollars.

explanation.correct: Right. The cost cap is roughly $215 million per year per team, with carve-outs.
explanation.incorrect: The F1 cost cap is approximately $215 million per year per team, slightly up from the 2021 baseline.
explanation.sayThisLine: The cost cap is about $215 million per team per year.

lessons.title: Reading pace from practice
lessons.objective: Tell one-lap pace from race pace and spot sandbagging.

payload.prompt: What do Friday long runs tell you about a team's race pace?

situation.narrative: Friday practice: Team A is 0.4 seconds slower in the Friday long run (steady pace for 15 laps) than in qualifying simulations (one-lap peak pace).

options.label: Their race pace is weak; expect them to fade from a good qualifying grid
options.consequence: Correct. Qualifying and race pace are different. Fast on Saturday, struggling on Sunday.
considerations: 0.4 seconds is a big gap
Tyres or balance cost them in the long run
If they qualify high, they may not defend the position

options.label: The gap is just fuel load; race pace is fine
options.consequence: Partial. Fuel load is part of it, but 0.4 seconds is still real pace loss.
considerations: Fuel does affect pace
But the gap suggests a handling issue that matters for the race

payload.expertNote: Friday long runs are the first hint of race pace. A 0.4-second gap between one-lap and race pace is significant.
payload.sayThisLine: Long runs show who has race pace, not just qualifying pace.

payload.prompt: How can you spot if a team is sandbagging (hiding pace) in practice?

situation.narrative: Friday practice: Team B runs on high fuel loads all day and posts only 12th-fastest on the timing sheet. Saturday they are on pole.

options.label: They were sandbagging: hiding pace with heavy fuel and setup choices to mislead rivals
options.consequence: Correct. A jump from 12th to pole is not just tyres or fuel; it is a deliberate pace hide.
considerations: Heavy fuel hides one-lap pace
Defensive setup in practice does not show qualifying speed
Saturday qualifying fuel and setup is totally different

options.label: It is just tyres and fuel; no sandbagging
options.consequence: Partially right. Tyres and fuel matter, but the gap is big enough to show intentional hiding.
considerations: Fuel load is part of it
But jumping that far suggests strategy, not just fuel

payload.expertNote: Sandbagging is intentional. Teams run heavy, stale tyres or a loose setup on Friday to hide their true pace.
payload.sayThisLine: Sandbagging: hiding pace with fuel and strategy on Friday.

payload.prompt: What is the difference between one-lap (qualifying) pace and race pace?

options.text: Qualifying is peak power over one lap; race pace is consistent speed over a stint with tyre management.
options.explanation: Right. Qualifying = one-lap peak. Race = tyre life and fuel load over 20-30 laps.

options.text: They are the same; a fast car is fast both ways.
options.explanation: No, a car can be quick on one lap but struggle over a long run. Different priorities.

options.text: Race pace is always faster because the car is lighter on fuel.
options.explanation: No, a car on light fuel in qualifying is fastest. Race pace includes fuel weight.

options.text: Qualifying pace depends only on the driver; race pace depends on the team.
options.explanation: Both depend on driver and car. The metrics are different, but both involve the whole team.

explanation.correct: Right. Qualifying is one-lap flat-out. Race pace is stamina: hold your pace while tyres age and fuel load decreases.
explanation.incorrect: Qualifying pace is peak one-lap speed. Race pace is sustained speed over a stint while managing tyres and fuel.

payload.prompt: A team qualifies 3rd but finishes 6th on Sunday. What does that tell you?

options.text: Their race pace is weaker than their one-lap pace; they faded after struggling with tyre wear or balance.
options.explanation: Right. Good qualifying, poor race result, means the car works for one lap but not over 70.

options.text: The driver made a mistake or was unlucky.
options.explanation: Maybe, but a 3-to-6 drop usually points to a pace issue, not just one mistake.

options.text: The team used the wrong tyres.
options.explanation: Tyre choice can affect it, but the gap suggests a fundamental pace issue in race conditions.

options.text: It means nothing; results vary race to race.
options.explanation: A big drop from grid to finish is a clear signal about race pace versus qualifying pace.

explanation.correct: Right. Grid position (qualifying) vs finishing position (race) tells the story of one-lap vs race pace.
explanation.incorrect: A drop from 3rd on the grid to 6th at the end signals weak race pace relative to qualifying.
